insight.title: Termite Mounds Ventilate Using Wind and Physics
insight.subtitle: Subterranean insect colonies maintain precise indoor climates through self-regulating mud towers.
insight.notificationHook: Termite mounds breathe without moving parts

sections.text: In scorching savannas, subterranean termite colonies keep their underground fungus farms at a constant climate. They achieve this without electricity or fans, even while external temperatures swing by forty degrees daily.

The mud towers function as giant passive lungs. Wind blowing across upper vents creates suction, pulling stale carbon dioxide up from deep below while drawing cool, oxygen-rich air through lower side tunnels.

By sculpting soil into precise thermal flues, termites convert external heat and wind currents into continuous circulation. Pure geometry drives an invisible, self-balancing HVAC system that never shuts down.
Mastery of climate control, achieved without a single moving part.

audioBrief.script:
Welcome to your Sift Daily Briefing. Here is the clear, plain version of today's top stories.

First, factory growth across Asia slowed down in October as chip demand met higher fuel costs. Surveys released on November second showed manufacturing slowed in China, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan. The Middle East war has kept fuel and food prices high across the region. China's manufacturing purchasing index fell to 52 in October from 52.1 in September. Japan's manufacturing index eased to 53.3 in October, its slowest expansion in seven months. South Korea's index dropped to 51.3, while Taiwan's index fell to 54.9. However, factory activity expanded faster in Vietnam, Indonesia, and Malaysia. The International Monetary Fund expects Asia's economy to grow 4.8 percent in 2026. The group projects growth will slow to 4.4 percent in 2027.

Turning to business, Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco reported a 34.5 percent profit jump. Net profit for the third quarter reached 36.25 billion dollars, up from 26.9 billion dollars last year. Aramco is the world's largest oil exporter. Higher global oil prices offset reduced output caused by the ongoing war between the United States and Iran. Brent crude oil averaged over 90 dollars a barrel during the quarter. Yemen's Houthi militants have launched waves of attacks against Saudi energy infrastructure and Aramco's headquarters. To maintain exports, Aramco ramped up crude shipments from its main hub at Ras Tanura in September. The company continued shipping crude oil out to global markets in November.

In trade news, United States import tariffs are creating friction with factory hubs across Southeast Asia. President Donald Trump announced broad import taxes in April 2025. The Supreme Court struck down much of that initial tariff regime in February. The administration then used emergency trade measures and launched investigations into forced labor and overcapacity. For a decade, companies moved factories out of China into Vietnam, Malaysia, India, and the Philippines. Trade policy expert Deborah Elms said Washington created alternate supply routes and now penalizes partners for using them. United States ambassador to Singapore Anjani Sinha asked local business leaders to double U.S. investments. Business leaders rejected the demand, and capital flows are pivoting further into Asia instead.

Next, asset manager Brookfield plans to build a large artificial intelligence data center in England. Brookfield signed an agreement with energy company Drax Group to build the facility in North Yorkshire. The data center will sit on the site of the Drax Power Station estate. Shares of Drax Group jumped 8.2 percent in early trading after the announcement. The project initially targets up to 100 megawatts of capacity starting in early 2028. Developers plan to add another 500 megawatts between 2028 and 2031. They eventually plan to secure more than one gigawatt of capacity at the site. Brookfield estimates total investment for the project could exceed 26.8 billion dollars. Phase one will require an initial investment of 2.5 billion pounds.

In health news, annual health insurance premiums for workers are expected to rise sharply next year. Analysts predict job-based health coverage premiums will jump up to 9.5 percent in 2027. Average family plan costs reached 28,303 dollars this year, according to non-profit KFF. Workers paid an average of 7,470 dollars toward those family health plans. Health policy experts say rising prices set by hospitals and drug companies drive up premium costs. Between 2002 and 2020, over 1,000 hospitals merged, reducing competition in local markets. During that time, the Federal Trade Commission took enforcement action in only 13 instances. The Centers for Disease Control says more people used prescription drugs in 2025 than in 2019.

Finally, Australia's High Court began hearing arguments over the country's social media ban for children. Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project argued in court on Tuesday that the law is unconstitutional. Australia passed the ban last December for ten social media platforms, including Facebook and TikTok. The law requires platforms to take reasonable steps to block users under 16 years old. Companies face fines up to 70 million US dollars for serious or repeated breaches. Reddit's lawyer Perry Herzfeld argued the ban restricts children from vital modern communication tools. Communications Minister Anika Wells defended the policy outside the court in Canberra. No social media company has been fined since the ban began. Government lawyer Joanna Davidson presents her defense of the policy on Wednesday.

Next, Europe's fridges are getting hacked, and we look at whether America could be next.

Supermarkets across Europe were hit by suspected cyber-attacks on their fridges and freezers. The attacks happened in November and raised concerns about internet-connected hardware. Researchers from UK Cyber Defence found more than 800 British retail control systems online. These systems handle refrigeration and building controls over the public internet. Tom Hegel, a researcher at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, warned about remote control risks. He said changing settings can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt computers. In May 2025, ransomware attacks hit British supermarkets M&S and the Co-op. Those attacks left store shelves empty of fresh deliveries for days. Since April 2024, UK law has set minimum cybersecurity standards for smart devices. Former cyber chief Ciaran Martin advises users to enable multi-factor authentication.

Turning to international economics, Ethiopia's economy is growing despite renewed fighting in the north. The International Monetary Fund forecasts economic growth of 9.2 percent for 2025 to 2026. Financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed warns that major conflict could stop this growth. A World Bank assessment puts damage from earlier conflicts at more than 22.6 billion dollars. Reconstruction costs for the country are estimated at approximately 19.7 billion dollars. The IMF forecasts an average inflation rate of 11.7 percent for 2025 to 2026. Ethiopia also defaulted on a Eurobond interest payment in late 2023. The government is following economic reforms under an IMF program launched in 2024.

In business news, Shell agreed to sell its stake in an Australian gas project for 1.45 billion dollars. The buyer is XRG, the energy investment arm of Abu Dhabi's state oil producer. XRG is buying the stake in the North West Shelf liquefied natural gas project. The facility has capacity to liquefy 14.3 million tonnes of gas each year. That capacity represents almost 3 percent of global total liquefied natural gas capacity. Shell sold its 16.67 percent stake as it transitions into a fee-based facility. The deal includes an extra payment linked to future gas field developments. Woodside Energy Group operates the plant alongside BP and other international partners.

Moving to energy policy, Indonesia announced it is unlikely to export electricity in the near future. Minister Bahlil Lahadalia cited high domestic demand for prioritizing local electricity needs. He said exports will only proceed if buyer countries agree to Indonesian prices. Last month, Indonesia reduced natural gas exports to Singapore by 31 million cubic feet daily. That cut represents about 8 percent of gas exports to Singapore. Bahlil stated that cutting 10 percent would be required to breach their contract. Natural gas currently generates about 95 percent of Singapore's electricity. The diverted gas is now powering regional grids in Batam, Bintan, and Sumatra.

Turning to technology, American chipmaker Nvidia relied on Chinese suppliers to build components for humanoid robots. Nvidia's humanoid robot systems feature mechanical hands made by China-linked startups.

In trade news, India is launching an initiative to boost exports from districts across the country. The government aims to narrow its trade deficit by helping local businesses export products. The initiative focuses on promoting farm products, textiles, footwear, and engineering goods. District councils held planning meetings across 120 districts between June and August 2026. First-time exporters obtained 32,000 export registration codes in 113 of those districts. Small and medium enterprises accounted for 65 percent of the new export codes. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said recent trade pacts added 60 trillion dollars in market access. India also extended special trade insurance coverage for exporters until March 31, 2027.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

In hot savannas, subterranean termites keep underground fungus farms at a constant climate. Outside temperatures swing by 40 degrees daily, but termites use no electricity or fans. Instead, their mud towers function as giant passive lungs. Wind blowing across upper vents creates suction to pull stale carbon dioxide upward. At the same time, cool air enters through lower side tunnels. The termites shape soil into flues, using natural wind to run a self-balancing cooling system. It is remarkable how complex climate control exists without a single moving part. How might human engineers use simple natural shapes to cool our own buildings?

Thank you for listening to the Sift Daily Briefing, and have a wonderful day.

audioBriefIndepth.script:
Welcome to your Sift In-Depth Briefing. Today we bring you the full analysis of three important economic stories shaping our world.

Why is factory growth slowing across Asia even with huge demand for artificial intelligence technology? Asian factory growth slowed because a war in the Middle East drove up fuel and food prices. 

Asia is the main center for making computer chips and high-tech electronic equipment. Factories in South Korea, Taiwan, and Japan make small parts that power modern devices. Recently, technology companies started building powerful artificial intelligence software. These new tools require millions of highly advanced computer chips to function. That need created a huge boom in chip orders for Asian factories over recent years. However, factories need cheap imported fuel to generate electricity and ship goods overseas. 

A war involving the United States, Israel, and Iran broke out in the Middle East. Private business surveys showed factory growth slowed across major Asian chip exporters in October. Analysts track factory growth using a reading called a purchasing managers index. A score above fifty shows growth, while a score below fifty means activity is shrinking. A survey by S and P Global showed China's factory index fell to 52 in October. That score was down from 52.1 in September. Official data showed China's factory activity shrank for the third time in four months. Economist Nguyen Hoang Nam from Capital Economics noted a sharp drop in construction activity. Japan's factory index eased to 53.3 in October from 54.1 in September. South Korea's index fell to 51.3 from 53.9 in September. Taiwan's index stood at 54.9 in October, down from 56.7 in September. Meanwhile, factory activity expanded faster in Vietnam, Indonesia, and Malaysia. India's manufacturing growth slowed down, but strong export orders helped cushion the drop. Toru Nishihama at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute said high inflation hurts Asian consumer spending. 

High fuel and food costs lasted long enough to offset strong global tech demand. The International Monetary Fund expects Asia's economy to grow 4.8 percent in 2026. Growth is projected to slow further to 4.4 percent in 2027. Japan's central bank warned that a crash in AI demand could harm exports and production. Watch to see if high energy prices continue to slow down global manufacturing.

Let us turn next to the Middle East, where major energy flows are shifting.

How did Saudi Arabia's state oil company make higher profits while producing less oil? Saudi Aramco earned more profit because global oil prices surged during recent war conflicts. 

Saudi Arabia relies heavily on energy sales to fund its government budget and public spending. Its state-owned oil firm, Aramco, is the largest crude oil exporter in the world. Aramco usually exports crude oil using ships traveling through the Persian Gulf and Red Sea. For years, Yemen's Houthi militants have launched missile and drone attacks against Saudi energy sites. 

Severe attacks damaged Saudi pipelines, forcing Aramco to move more shipments through the Persian Gulf. Aramco reported a third-quarter net profit of 36.25 billion dollars. That was a 34.5 percent increase from 26.9 billion dollars a year earlier. Adjusted net income reached 31.2 billion dollars, beating an analyst consensus of 30.66 billion dollars. Total liquid production dropped about 10 percent to 8.7 million barrels a day. However, Aramco sold its oil at 95.20 dollars a barrel, up from 70.10 dollars. Brent crude oil averaged over 90 dollars a barrel during the third quarter. Oil prices topped 100 dollars a barrel by the middle of September. Downstream earnings from refineries and trading jumped over three-fold to more than 10 billion dollars. Aramco maintained its base dividend payout at 21.9 billion dollars for the quarter. The company's gearing, which measures company debt against capital, eased to 5.5 percent. Houthi attacks hit Aramco's East-West pipeline, Yanbu terminals, refineries, an oil field, and company headquarters. 

Escalating war between the United States and Iran raised fears of major oil shipping disruptions. Higher energy income gives the Saudi government essential funds to support its public economy. Watch to see if future militant attacks disrupt crucial Saudi export routes in the Gulf.

Moving on to global trade, American policies are changing how Asian nations do business.

Why are American trade tariffs pushing Southeast Asian nations closer to business with China? American import taxes hurt regional partners, encouraging Asian countries to build trade networks without Washington. 

For decades, the United States built strong economic alliances across Asia to balance Chinese power. American leaders encouraged companies to move factories out of China into friendly Southeast Asian countries. This strategy was widely known as the China plus one approach. Nations like Vietnam, Malaysia, and the Philippines became vital new manufacturing hubs for global firms. American companies invested heavily in these markets to protect supply chains from political risks. 

President Donald Trump announced broad import tariffs that hit manufacturers across Southeast Asia. In February, the Supreme Court struck down much of the initial tariff regime. The administration then used Section 122 emergency measures and broad Section 301 investigations. Regional exporters, American importers, and everyday consumers absorbed the higher costs of these taxes. Former diplomat Evan Feigenbaum said Washington is executing a reverse pivot out of Asia. Trade expert Deborah Elms noted Washington penalized regional partners for using alternative supply routes. Ambassador Anjani Sinha told Singapore leaders to double U.S. investments, but business leaders rejected the demand. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned that weaponized economic tools force middle powers to organize together. Southeast Asian nations are now joining regional trade groups like RCEP and CPTPP without Washington. Eleven nations are creating the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement for a two trillion dollar market. Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore remain among America's top twenty trading partners. 

Washington focused on short-term trade coercion instead of building reliable rules with regional allies. Southeast Asian nations may design future digital and trade rules that bypass American influence. Watch to see if Asian countries expand economic ties with China while U.S. influence declines.

Next up, Brookfield targets a 27 billion dollar AI data center at a power station.

Why are companies rushing to borrow billions of dollars to build data centers for artificial intelligence? The boom is driving a massive wave of debt, and it has already flooded global markets with more than six hundred fifty billion dollars of borrowing since the start of twenty twenty five. 

Data center operators build giant warehouses packed with powerful computers. These computers run complex artificial intelligence software that needs huge amounts of electricity and space. 

Companies want to cash in on this new technology, so they need to build more data centers quickly. Building these large centers costs a lot of money, which means companies have to borrow from banks to pay for construction. 

This brings us to Singapore based data centre operator STT GDC. The company builds and runs data centers across twelve countries, including India, Japan, the United Kingdom, and Italy. 

A group led by investment firm KKR and Singapore Telecommunications agreed to buy STT GDC for six point six billion Singapore dollars. The buyers completed this purchase in September. They used a five billion dollar sustainability linked loan to help pay for the deal. 

Now, STT GDC is back in the market for more money. The company is in talks with banks for a three point one billion Singapore dollar syndicated loan, which is a large loan shared by a group of multiple banks. 

This three year loan pays an interest margin of one hundred sixty five basis points over the benchmark Singapore Overnight Rate Average. It also comes with an extension option of up to two years. The proceeds will be used as financing for STT GDC assets. 

Banks working on this planned borrowing include Standard Chartered, United Overseas Bank, Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation, and DBS Bank. Representatives from STT GDC, Standard Chartered, DBS, KKR, and UOB declined to comment. Singtel and OCBC did not respond to requests for comment. 

This new deal happens because the artificial intelligence boom continues to fuel high demand for debt among companies building digital infrastructure. This ongoing borrowing binge has raised worries among investors. The heavy borrowing pushes up bond yields and increases scrutiny of what many see as lofty valuations of companies linked to artificial intelligence. 

Looking ahead, Moody’s Ratings expects at least three trillion dollars of data centre related investments over the next five years. If borrowing costs keep rising, companies might find it harder to fund these massive projects, which could slow down how fast new artificial intelligence infrastructure gets built. 

Why are everyday Americans paying so much more for their health insurance? Experts say workers will face sharp price jumps next year, with premiums expected to rise as much as nine point five percent in twenty twenty seven. 

Most working Americans get their health insurance through their jobs. Employers buy these plans from insurance companies and share the cost with their workers. 

Over the years, the cost of delivering medical care has steadily climbed. Hospitals and drug makers set their own prices without much regulation, so competition is supposed to keep costs down. 

Instead, many hospitals and doctor practices have merged into larger systems. More than one thousand hospitals merged between two thousand two and twenty twenty, and the Federal Trade Commission took enforcement action in only thirteen instances. These mergers often let companies raise prices because they no longer face local competitors. 

This brings us to today's rising expenses for the one hundred fifty seven million Americans who get health insurance through work. The average cost of an employer based family healthcare plan reached twenty eight thousand three hundred three dollars this year, which is a five percent increase from twenty twenty five. 

Workers contributed on average seven thousand four hundred seventy dollars annually, which is about nine percent more than last year. Analysts point to three main reasons for these increases. 

First, healthcare providers are charging patients more for care. Health spending accounted for ninety one percent of the growth in average premiums between twenty eleven and twenty four. 

Second, people are using more healthcare. Insurance companies are relying less on prior authorizations, which are rules where doctors must ask permission before a treatment. When companies dial back those rules, patients use more care. More people also used prescription drugs in twenty twenty five than in nineteen, and an aging population brings more chronic conditions. 

Third, new medications are driving up costs. Breakthrough drugs like GLP-1 agonists, which treat diabetes and obesity, are under patent and in high demand. A Gallup poll found eleven percent of Americans were using one of these medications in twenty twenty six, up from three percent in twenty twenty four. 

Even though fewer than one in five companies with two hundred or more employees offer coverage for these weight loss drugs, fifty six percent of companies say the medications have a significant impact on prescription drug spending. 

This is happening now because medical costs face a post pandemic bounceback while expensive new treatments flood the market. For the listener, this means employers may continue shifting more of the financial burden onto workers. Analysts suggest these costs could keep climbing unless lawmakers find ways to control overall healthcare spending. 

Can a government successfully ban teenagers from using social media? Australia's top court is now deciding if the world's first teen social media ban violates constitutional rights. 

Australia passed a landmark law to protect children from harmful online content. The law bans young people under sixteen years old from having accounts on large social media platforms. 

Supporters say the rule protects children from harm, but critics argue the ban is too blunt and restricts free speech. The law forces ten major platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Reddit, to take reasonable steps to keep under sixteen year olds off their sites. Platforms face fines of up to ninety nine million Australian dollars for serious breaches. 

This brings us to the High Court in Canberra. Reddit and a digital rights group called the Digital Freedom Project argued at a hearing that the law should be struck down as unconstitutional. 

Inside the courtroom, Reddit’s lawyer Perry Herzfeld told the full bench of the High Court that the law was ill thought out and inept. He argued that barring young people from holding accounts stops them from creating or responding to content on the most important means of communication in the modern world, which creates a profound restriction on political debate. 

Government lawyer Joanna Davidson defended the law, telling the court that social media harms children and that the government seeks to defend the right of children to be free from harm. 

Communications Minister Anika Wells spoke outside the court, calling the question of what society accepts from tech platforms the most compelling policy question of our time. 

This legal challenge is happening now because the Digital Freedom Project filed its constitutional challenge just weeks before the ban went live on December tenth of last year. 

For the listener, a successful court challenge could slow down similar policies being considered by lawmakers from Britain to Malaysia. If the ban survives, platforms may be forced to tighten their age verification systems, while teens will likely keep looking for ways around the rules. 

Europe's fridges are getting hacked. Could America be next?

If hackers take control of store freezers, how vulnerable is other technology? Supermarkets across Europe were hit by cyber-attacks that targeted their fridges and freezers.

Smart devices are everyday gadgets connected to the internet. These can include fridges, central heating, and washing machines. Connecting devices online makes them easier to control from far away. However, any device online can potentially be targeted by malicious hackers. Big brands generally work hard to make sure their tech is safe. In 2015, researchers showed a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge allowed traffic interception. That same year, experts remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system. The vehicle industry responded quickly and fixed that safety issue. Mobile connections also help engineers monitor equipment in power plants and water networks. In April 2024, UK law began requiring minimum cyber security standards for smart devices. These rules focus on stronger passwords and regular software updates. Then, in May 2025, ransomware hackers targeted British retailers M&S and the Co-op. Stores struggled to stock shop shelves with fresh food deliveries. Customers complained about empty shelves for days after the attack.

In November, suspected cyber-attacks hit supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe.

Shop freezers in seven European countries were affected by these cyber-attacks. There is no evidence domestic home appliances were targeted in these attacks. The UK National Cyber Security Centre said it is unaware of any UK impact. It is working with international partners and industry to understand the incidents. However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence identified over 800 retail control interfaces on the public internet. These systems control refrigeration and building settings for British retailers. That exposure could leave systems open to weak passwords or software vulnerabilities. Cyber security expert Ken Munro said UK utilities secure connections well, but global standards vary. He expressed concern for smaller, poorly funded utilities using older equipment. Cybersecurity expert Olivier Daloy warned that any factory connected to the internet faces risks. Tom Hegel from SentinelOne said retailers must decide who owns equipment security. He warned that changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just disrupt computers. Helen Dickinson from the British Retail Consortium said businesses are sharing intelligence with officials.

These attacks are happening now because attackers are finding exposed equipment linked to public internet networks.

This situation shows that internet-connected machinery can threaten physical goods like food supplies. Former cyber security chief Ciaran Martin suggests updating device software regularly. He also recommends using multi-factor authentication whenever possible. He admitted it is a pain, but noted it takes only a few seconds. Watch whether governments introduce stricter security laws for industrial internet systems.

While digital threats imperil European stores, physical conflict is threatening economic progress in Africa.

Will renewed fighting derail the strong economic recovery in Ethiopia? Ethiopia's economy is expanding rapidly, but renewed fighting in the north threatens that momentum.

A severe war raged in Tigray and other regions between 2020 and 2022. The violence destroyed infrastructure, reduced business output, and stopped farming in some areas. A World Bank assessment evaluated the damage from November 2020 to December 2021. It estimated conflict damage at over 22.6 billion dollars. Economic losses amounted to around 6 billion dollars. Reconstruction funding needs were estimated at approximately 19.7 billion dollars through 2028. Financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed noted the war caused high inflation and foreign currency shortages. In 2022, Ethiopia lost trade benefits under the United States African Growth and Opportunity Act. That law had allowed certain exports to enter the American market duty-free. The Pretoria peace agreement in November 2022 helped economic recovery begin. The International Monetary Fund reported economic growth of 7.2 percent in the 2022 to 2023 period. Growth reached 8.1 percent in 2023 to 2024. In late 2023, Ethiopia defaulted after missing an interest payment on a Eurobond. An IMF program launched in 2024 aimed to repair structural economic weaknesses.

Renewed fighting broke out in the north alongside crop problems caused by bad weather.

The IMF forecasts real economic growth of 9.2 percent for 2025 to 2026. Agriculture, mining, and electricity generation are driving this expansion. Gross domestic product measures overall output, so national growth can happen while specific regions suffer. However, Abdulmenan Mohammed warns that major conflict would make current growth unsustainable. He warned that military spending ties up money needed for infrastructure, education, and social services. The government may borrow more domestically, making it harder for private businesses to get credit. The IMF forecasts average inflation of 11.7 percent for 2025 to 2026. Mohammed warned that military demand for foreign currency reduces reserves for private imports. That puts pressure on the birr exchange rate and raises costs for imported fuel and goods. He highlighted agriculture and tourism as especially vulnerable sectors. Rural fighting disrupts farming, while poor rainfall reduces harvest yields and raises food prices. Security concerns also deter foreign tourists, cutting hotel and tour revenues. Currently, there is no evidence companies are leaving Ethiopia for Kenya.

The government faces this pressure now because military costs are rising alongside existing reconstruction bills.

Rising prices and uncertain incomes could create severe hardship for poorer Ethiopian households. It remains uncertain whether five-year reconstruction plans can be fully funded and completed. Watch whether the government can calm regional fighting and keep inflation under control.

Economic stability shapes national futures, while energy investments shape global business markets.

Why is a Middle Eastern energy company buying a big stake in an Australian gas plant? The investment arm of Abu Dhabi's state oil producer agreed to buy Shell's Australian gas stake.

Liquefied natural gas, or LNG, is gas chilled into liquid form for easy boat transport. Asian nations rely heavily on imported gas to generate electricity and run factories. Middle Eastern gas exporters historically shipped fuel directly from their home ports. However, conflicts in the Middle East severely disrupted energy flows out of the region. Those disruptions increased urgency for Gulf energy firms to buy assets around the world. Rival exporter Qatar also began expanding LNG operations outside the Middle East. Qatar wanted to reduce its exposure to potential blockades in the Strait of Hormuz. Abu Dhabi National Oil Company created an investment arm called XRG. XRG has been scouring the world for gas supplies to expand its business. The company aims to become one of the top five global LNG suppliers. XRG signed capacity agreements for gas projects in the United States and Argentina. In 2025, XRG attempted to purchase Australian gas producer Santos, but pulled its bid.

Shell decided to sell its stake in an Australian project as part of an operational change.

On Tuesday, XRG agreed to pay 1.45 billion dollars for Shell's stake in North West Shelf. North West Shelf is Australia's oldest and largest natural gas liquefaction plant. The operator of the facility is Woodside Energy Group. Other partners include BP, CNOOC, and a venture between Mitsui and Mitsubishi. The plant can liquefy 14.3 million tonnes of gas every year. That capacity represents almost 3 percent of the global total for LNG. This agreement is XRG's first asset purchase in Australia. Shell holds a 16.67 percent stake in the project. Shell integrated gas president Cederic Cremers said the sale realizes value from a mature asset. Shell will also receive an additional milestone-linked contingent payment. That payment may depend on plans to develop the Browse gas fields. The plant is transitioning into a facility where buyers pay fees to process gas.

XRG made this move now to secure reliable fuel supplies for customers across Asia.

This purchase gives Abu Dhabi a permanent stronghold in the growing Asia-Pacific energy market. It protects XRG from energy shipping bottlenecks inside the Middle East. Watch whether XRG makes additional acquisitions to reach its top-five global goal.

Next, we look at why Indonesia is unlikely to export electricity in the near future.

Will Indonesia stop sending electricity across its borders soon? Indonesia is prioritizing its own power needs and is unlikely to export electricity anytime soon.

Indonesia has grown rapidly over recent decades. More factories and homes need stable electric power every year. To meet this need, the nation relies heavily on coal, water power, and natural gas. Nearby Singapore has very little land to build big power plants. Because of this, natural gas is used to generate about 95 percent of Singapore's electricity. For years, Singapore bought gas through pipelines directly from Indonesian islands. Singapore also wanted to buy low-carbon electricity from firms in Indonesia. Indonesian leaders previously granted conditional approvals to explore those sales. However, rapid domestic growth caused power demand inside Indonesia to surge. This created a choice between earning export money and supplying local factories.

Indonesia recently started cutting gas shipments to Singapore to fuel its own power plants.

Bahlil Lahadalia is Indonesia's Coordinating Minister for Downstreaming and Energy Transition. He also serves as Indonesia's energy and mineral resources minister. He announced that Indonesia will not export electricity in the near future. Speaking in Jakarta, he explained that domestic power needs remain very high. He stated that exports might happen if buyers agree to prices set by Indonesia. He warned the sovereign wealth fund Danantara not to give in to foreign lobbying. He stated that state authority and national sovereignty must come first. Indonesia recently reduced gas exports to Singapore by 31 million standard cubic feet per day. That move redirected 15 million units from Natuna and 16 million from Sumatra. Natuna gas went to PLN Batam through the WNTS to Pulau Pemping to Batam pipeline. Sumatra gas moved through the TGI pipeline to Batam, Bintan, and Sumatra. Bahlil said this eight percent reduction falls within normal contract limits. He noted that only a ten percent reduction would breach contracts. A Singapore ministry spokesperson said gas importer Gas Supply Private Limited is reviewing contract terms. The ministry welcomed clarifications that Indonesian suppliers will honour their contracts. Bahlil suggested some gas was resold abroad, but reports say he provided no evidence. Singapore clarified that traded gas usually ships directly without entering Singapore. ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn believes both nations can resolve the issue swiftly.

This shift is happening now because of routine maintenance and growing local electricity usage.

Regional energy security could feel the impact of these tighter fuel supplies. People should watch whether prospective buyer countries agree to the export prices set by Indonesia. If price terms are not met, electricity exports will remain on hold.

Now, let us turn to a quick update on advanced technology manufacturing.

Nvidia relied on Chinese suppliers to build components for humanoid robots. The United States chipmaker features mechanical hands from China-linked startups in its humanoid robot systems.

Next, we look at how India plans to boost its local businesses and trade.

Can local towns help India reduce its international trade gap? India is encouraging local districts across the nation to sell more goods to foreign buyers.

India has a large economy with hundreds of distinct local districts. For many years, India bought more goods from other countries than it sold abroad. This gap between spending and earning created a growing trade deficit. To fix this, the government wanted small factories and farms to join global trade. Many small makers produced great goods but did not know how to export them. The government created the One District One Product program to brand unique local items. By January 2026, a broader export hub plan covered over 770 districts nationwide. The goal was to transform local district strengths into foreign cash earnings. India also sought trade pacts with major nations to lower tariffs on Indian goods. Former trade agreements covered foreign economies worth ten trillion dollars in output. Expanding these trade networks helps small businesses find new customers overseas.

Local councils held trade meetings across 120 districts to help small firms start exporting.

In 113 of those districts, new exporters obtained 32,000 Importer Exporter Code registrations. Micro, small, and medium enterprises accounted for 65 percent of those new registration codes. The push promotes textiles, farm goods, footwear, engineering products, and specialty regional items. India is using three main tools to help these local businesses grow. The Districts as Export Hubs initiative provides guidance to new exporters. The Export Promotion Mission offers direct financial help to small firms. New free trade agreements give Indian exporters better access to foreign buyers. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said nine recent trade deals added 60 trillion dollars in market access. Those deals include pacts with the United States, Britain, Australia, and the European Union. Negotiations with Canada, Israel, and other blocs could add 15 trillion dollars more. Under the RELIEF initiative, India extended exporter insurance through March 2027.

India faces trade gaps and West Asia conflict, so it must expand local export choices.

More Indian goods could soon enter market shelves around the world. Observers should watch whether upcoming trade pact negotiations successfully open major new global markets. If these deals close, millions of small Indian workshops could expand their global sales.

Before we go, here is your thought for the day.

Deep beneath scorching savannas, subterranean termite colonies keep underground fungus farms at a constant climate. These underground farms need steady conditions to grow food for the colony. Outside on the savanna, daily temperatures swing by 40 degrees. Yet, termites manage their internal climate without using electricity or mechanical fans. They accomplish this by building tall mud towers above their underground tunnels. These mud towers function as giant passive lungs for the colony. When wind blows across the upper vents, it creates a powerful suction effect. That suction pulls stale carbon dioxide up from deep below the ground. Meanwhile, cool air is drawn inward through lower side tunnels. This fresh air brings vital oxygen down into the subterranean colony. By sculpting soil into precise thermal flues, termites convert external heat and wind into continuous circulation. Pure geometry drives an invisible, self-balancing climate control system. The system works day and night and never shuts down. The insects achieve total climate mastery without a single moving part. It is amazing how living creatures use basic physics to solve difficult engineering problems. How could human designers use natural shapes to cool cities without relying on power grids?

Thank you for spending time with Sift In-Depth today. Until next time, take care and stay curious.
